fact_sheet.business_description: American Express combines a recognized travel-payments franchise with financial-services activities including IDS [D01]. The business centers on a charge-card brand linking cardholders, merchants, and a promise to pay [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Charge-card products and financial services; customers rely on the brand's promise to pay and merchant acceptance [D01]
economics: Travel payments combine service charges with float (funds held between receipt and settlement) [D01]; pretax margins 4.7%/6.3%/17.5% for 1991-93 [D02]; return on tangible operating capital varies by segment [D06]
earnings_record: 1989-1993 net income: $1,157/$181/$789/$461/$1,478 million [D02]; Adjusted continuing EPS for 1991-93: $1.21/$0.23/$2.30 [D02]; 1993 includes a $433 million gain [D02]
competitive_position: Brand is a recognized travel-payments franchise; integrated service model; competition includes other bank-issued payment networks [D01, D06]
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Short and long debt: $21,050 million (1993) [D02]; Tier-1 capital 6.6%, total capital 13.0% (June 1994) [D06]; deposits/settlement funding are not unencumbered cash [D02]
management_and_capital_allocation: Harvey Golub's leadership; focus on payments/financial services and away from unfocused conglomerate [D01]; 1993 dividend $1.00 [D02]
price_and_valuation: Common quote $26.50 (July 1994) [D04]; P/E 11.52x based on 1993 adjusted EPS [D04]; P/B 2.24x [D04]; indicated dividend yield 3.40% [D04]
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Competitive card networks, merchant resistance to fees, consumer credit exposure, and potential failure of the restructuring [D05]
deal_terms_if_any: $300 million 8.85% preferred (1991); conversion features include a cap at $414 million and no floor [D02]
recent_events: June 1994 quarter: $359 million continuing net income [D03]; cards total 35.6 million [D03]
berkshire_context: Existing exposure via preferred/common; Berkshire already has experience with the issuer; no specific new allocation decision in pack [D07, D08]
missing_data: Complete current cash-flow reconciliation, current full-year earnings guidance, and peer P/E/P/B valuation grid

understandable.evidence: The company operates a recognized, long-standing travel-payments franchise that customers rely on for reliability and merchant acceptance [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The business possesses a strong brand and an integrated service model that facilitates travel payments and merchant networks [D01, D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: While 1991-1993 results were impacted by restructuring, core franchise performance shows recovery with $1,478 million in net income in 1993, and one-time charges do not invalidate the core business record [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The company maintains solid capital ratios with 13% total capital and operates a financial model where funding is sourced through deposits and settlement flows rather than traditional debt [D02, D06].

capital_intensity.evidence: As a financial services and payments business, it does not require significant physical capital to grow its network [D01].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Harvey Golub has demonstrated discipline by refocusing the company on its core payments business and away from an unfocused conglomerate [D01].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: With earnings over $1 billion and a large market presence, the company is of sufficient scale for Berkshire's portfolio [D02].

price_screen.evidence: Trading at approximately 11.5x earnings with a dividend yield of 3.4% represents a reasonable valuation relative to long-term government bond benchmarks [D04].

conflicts_resolved: Book value: used $16.81 consolidated figure as it represents the current GAAP accounting base before pro-forma adjustments [D02].
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a powerful payments franchise with a durable brand and high-margin recurring revenue

gate2.why_available: The market remains skeptical due to past earnings volatility and concerns over competitive pressure from bank-issued networks. We believe the franchise remains durable and that Golub's refocusing efforts will allow the core payments business to produce normalized, high-margin earnings that the market currently fails to fully value [D01, D02, D05].
evidence: Core franchise performance shows recovery with $1,478 million in 1993 net income [D02]
Customers continue to rely on the brand's promise to pay and global merchant acceptance [D01]
Restructuring is successfully refocusing the company on payments and away from unfocused activities [D01]
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market fears merchant resistance to fees and competitive card networks will permanently impair the company's earnings power [D05].
what_must_be_true: The core card-member base remains loyal to the brand's service model
Merchant acceptance stays high despite fee pressures
Restructuring effectively removes non-core, lower-return distractions
Management maintains capital discipline and conservative credit standards

gate3.price_vs_value: 95% of low-end value; modest margin of safety
gate3.alternatives: Existing Berkshire holdings and cash equivalents remain the benchmark; current Amex price is fair but lacks the extreme margin of safety required for a major new capital allocation [D07]
gate3.downside_case: Continued erosion of fee income due to competitive network pressure; not permanent loss of capital given franchise durability, but significant impairment of growth prospects
flagged_assumptions: Normalized EPS assumed at $1.75 based on trailing 1993/1994 run-rate excluding one-time gains [D02, D03]
Assumed cost of capital/discount rate 7.5% per standard market context for 1994

gate4.role_description: We are a permanent passive holder. We do not look for a catalyst to unlock value, preferring to own a wonderful business that compounds over time [D01].
value_realisation_path: Business compounding through the core payments franchise [D01].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: For the 1980-1999 period, we seek high-quality consumer franchises to hold for the long term, avoiding the active restructuring and control mandates of our early partnership era [D01, instructions].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power due to successful aggressive discounting by competing bank-issued networks
Management departs from the core payments strategy to pursue unrelated acquisitions
Credit losses significantly exceed historical normalized levels, impairing capital ratios below regulatory minimums
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain sufficient liquidity for insurance operations and existing commitments; requires regulatory approval for holdings exceeding 10% of banking institutions [D06].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Incremental capital allocation into existing high-quality consumer franchises or the repurchase of Berkshire stock if trading below intrinsic value.
gate5.decider_reason: American Express is a core consumer franchise within my circle of competence, and the position size is consistent with a major, long-term Buffett-managed allocation.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The erosion of the travel-payments franchise's competitive moat through persistent, successful fee undercutting by bank-issued card networks.

valuation.downside_case: Continued erosion of fee income due to competitive pressure, leading to stagnation of growth but not permanent loss of capital.

drivers.driver: The company trades at a price of $26.50 against an intrinsic value range of $28 to $35, providing a margin of safety [D02, D04].
American Express operates a powerful, durable payments franchise with a unique brand and global merchant acceptance that customers rely on [D01, D06].
Management under Harvey Golub has successfully refocused the company on its core payments business, shedding non-core distractions [D01].
The business model generates high-margin recurring revenue with limited capital intensity compared to traditional industrial operations [D01, D06].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power due to successful aggressive discounting by competing bank-issued networks
Management departs from the core payments strategy to pursue unrelated acquisitions
Credit losses significantly exceed historical normalized levels, impairing capital ratios below regulatory minimums
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that the competitive moat is permanently impaired by rival networks, or that the company can no longer maintain its cardholder loyalty and premium pricing power.
final.memo:
American Express is a franchise that Charlie and I have long admired, centering on a global payments network that links cardholders and merchants through a trusted promise to pay [D01]. We understand the business well: it is a service-oriented model that relies on brand integrity and global acceptance rather than heavy industrial plant [D01, D06].

Despite recent industry noise, the company maintains a formidable moat built on deep-seated customer habits and the essential utility of its network [D01, D05]. While 1991-1993 results were noisy due to restructuring, the core business generated $1,478 million in net income in 1993, demonstrating the earnings power of a streamlined payments focus [D02].

Harvey Golub has done a commendable job refocusing the company on its core strengths, moving away from an unfocused conglomerate structure [D01]. This transition indicates an owner-minded approach to capital allocation that prioritizes long-term franchise value over short-term diversification [D01].

Mr. Market currently seems preoccupied with competitive pressures and past earnings volatility, which has created an opportunity for us to acquire shares at $26.50, a level that sits below our conservative intrinsic value estimate [D04, D05]. We believe this price offers a sufficient margin of safety given the durability of the brand [D03].

We value the business at $28 to $35 per share based on normalized earnings potential of $1.75 [D02, D03]. We anticipate a reasonable return from this level, viewing it as a permanent hold that benefits from the compounding nature of the global payments industry [D01, D03].

Our primary risk is the potential erosion of the moat via persistent fee undercutting by bank-issued competitors [D05]. We will cap our initial investment at 5% of the equity portfolio to reflect our standard entry sizing for a high-quality consumer franchise within our circle of competence [D05].
